item.title: Critical Java Vulnerability Requires Immediate Patching
item.description:
Purpose

CISA strongly urges organizations to immediately patch the recently disclosed Oracle Java vulnerability CVE-2026-114938. This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as “Java4Shell,” affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK). Specially crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM and allow for unauthenticated remote code execution.

Actions to take

CISA urges organizations to take the following actions:

  • Identify affected Java installations. Review your software inventory for JDKs and Java runtimes, including those bundled with third-party applications or included in container images and appliances. Note: JDKs and Java runtimes may not appear as separate entries in software inventories.
  • Apply relevant Java and vendor patches as soon as they are available, prioritizing internet-facing systems.
    • If immediate patching is not feasible, implement temporary compensating controls, such as restricting and validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits, and limiting unauthenticated access.
  • Review Oracle’s security advisory for guidance on patching and affected products and versions.
  •  Monitor for indicators of suspicious activity, including rogue runtimes, unexpected JVM crashes, and suspicious Java processes.

CISA urges network defenders to review the following resource and apply necessary updates:

  • Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.

  • When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

item.title: Yemen: Yémen : au moins 64 enfants ont été tués et 64 autres blessés depuis l’intensification des hostilités il y a près de trois mois
item.description:
Country: Yemen
Source: UN Children's Fund

NEW YORK, le 18 novembre 2026 – Au moins 64 enfants ont été tués et 64 autres blessés au Yémen depuis l’intensification des hostilités le 3 septembre dernier. Ce bilan devrait encore s’alourdir alors que les combats se poursuivent aux abords de zones densément peuplées, notamment à Taëz et à Lahj.

« L’augmentation du nombre d’enfants tués et blessés au Yémen est bouleversante. Cela doit cesser », a déclaré Catherine Russell, Directrice générale de l’UNICEF. « Derrière chaque chiffre se cache un enfant dont la vie a été fauchée ou bouleversée à jamais. »

Les services essentiels et les infrastructures dont dépendent les enfants sont eux aussi directement touchés. Au moins sept écoles et 28 établissements de santé, dont cinq soutenus par l’UNICEF, ont été endommagés depuis le début de cette escalade. Le 2 novembre, une attaque contre le centre de santé d’Al-Suqyah à Lahj, soutenu par l’UNICEF et desservant environ 1 700 personnes, aurait par ailleurs fait cinq morts, dont trois professionnels de santé.

Parallèlement, les déplacements de population s’intensifient. Plus de 330 000 personnes, dont environ 174 000 enfants, ont été déplacées depuis la reprise des hostilités. De nombreuses familles trouvent refuge dans des bâtiments inachevés ou endommagés et peinent à accéder à la nourriture, à l’eau potable et aux soins de santé.

La situation dans la ville de Taëz est particulièrement alarmante. Alors que la route principale reliant Aden est fermée et que les itinéraires alternatifs sont peu sûrs, plus de 800 000 personnes étaient privées d’aide humanitaire à la fin du mois d’octobre, selon les informations disponibles. La production d’eau a chuté de près de 50 %, les prix des denrées alimentaires et du carburant ont plus que doublé, et les pénuries de médicaments, de carburant, d’oxygène médical et d’électricité perturbent fortement les soins d’urgence, ainsi que les soins maternels et néonatals.

Dans les zones touchées par l’escalade du conflit, plus de 1 160 écoles ont fermé leurs portes ou suspendu les cours, une situation qui affecte plus d’un demi-million d’élèves. Par ailleurs, près d’un enfant sur trois parmi ceux récemment examinés par les équipes mobiles de santé de l’UNICEF souffre de malnutrition aiguë. La surpopulation dans les sites d’accueil, le manque de latrines et l’accès limité à l’eau potable augmentent également le risque de propagation des maladies.

Face à ce contexte, l’UNICEF renforce son intervention d’urgence afin de venir en aide à près de 350 000 personnes. L’organisation redéploie des équipes mobiles de santé et de nutrition vers les sites d’accueil des personnes déplacées et les communautés touchées à Aden, Lahj, Abyan, Marib et Taëz, intensifie son soutien d’urgence en matière d’approvisionnement en eau et d’assainissement, fournit un soutien psychosocial et assure une prise en charge individualisée des cas, notamment pour les enfants non accompagnés ou séparés de leur famille.

« Les enfants au Yémen ont déjà beaucoup trop souffert. Il est urgent que les équipes humanitaires puissent les atteindre en toute sécurité et sans entrave », a ajouté Catherine Russell. « Toutes les parties doivent respecter les obligations mises à leur charge par le droit international. Les enfants doivent être protégés et pouvoir accéder aux services essentiels dont ils dépendent, notamment aux soins de santé, à l’éducation, à l’eau potable et à la nourriture. »

item.title: World: How AI is helping to reinforce polio surveillance in Africa
item.description:
Country: World
Source: Global Polio Eradication Initiative

**Brazzaville—** Every week, the polio eradication programme at the World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for Africa receives surveillance and operational data from the region’s 47 countries. From poliovirus detections and laboratory results to vaccination campaign coverage and health facility visits, this information is essential to guiding outbreak response and reaching every child. But with growing volumes of data spread across different platforms, turning information into actionable insights has not always been straightforward.

Until recently, producing a district-level map or country summary often involved several manual steps: locating datasets, cleaning and combining information, and generating maps, charts and reports. During an outbreak, teams could spend valuable time waiting for an analyst to provide the information they needed to make decisions.

The WHO Africa’s Geographic Information Systems (GIS) Centre is changing this through the integration of AI into its operational dashboards. Instead of navigating multiple databases or relying on technical expertise, programme officers can now ask questions in plain language and receive relevant maps, charts or tables directly from the dashboards.

For example, an officer can request a breakdown of circulating variant poliovirus type 2 (cVDPV2) detections by district in a specific country since January 2026. The system retrieves the relevant information and presents it in an accessible visual format, allowing users to explore trends by location, reporting period or virus type. The Poliovirus Detection Dashboard also features an AI-powered query function that generates written summaries from current and archived records, supported by relevant figures. This reduces the time spent on manual data extraction and reporting, allowing teams to focus more on interpreting findings, verifying information and following up on priority areas.

“AI-supported analysis is enabling the program to strengthen the monitoring of poliovirus detections and analysis of vaccination coverage and campaign quality while also enhancing surveillance monitoring through the Integrated Supportive Supervision (ISS) and eSURV Visits. By bringing together data across the different interventions, the program is able to identify potential surveillance gaps and identify areas with suboptimal campaign performance requiring closer attention and follow-up,” says Dr Kebba Touray, Head of the WHO Africa’s GIS Centre.

Similar capabilities are being extended to campaign monitoring, helping programme teams identify delayed supplementary immunization activities (SIAs), understand reported reasons for delays and address operational bottlenecks.

As the world marks GIS Day on 18 November, these innovations reflect how GIS is evolving beyond traditional mapping. By combining geographical information with AI-powered analysis, WHO AFRO is helping public health teams move from simply visualizing where cases occur to identifying patterns, understanding gaps and determining where action is needed most.

AI does not replace epidemiological expertise or human verification. Rather, it gives health professionals faster access to information, enabling them to make better-informed decisions and respond more effectively to public health threats.

This GIS Day, WHO Africa highlights the growing role of geospatial innovation in advancing polio eradication. Because behind every map, dataset and analysis is a shared objective: ensuring that the right information reaches the right people at the right time to help protect every child from polio.

item.title: A study of 26 due diligence systems in Ukraine shows how donors can reduce duplicate checks for civil society organisations
item.description:
Country: Ukraine
Source: Philanthropy in Ukraine

Please refer to the attached file.

Philanthropy in Ukraine compared 26 due diligence systems used by international donors and organisations. In 193 of 650 comparisons, one donor’s assessment already covers more than 80% of another donor’s requirements. This creates opportunities for donors to recognise each other’s assessments and reduce the administrative burden on Ukrainian civil society organisations.

Ukrainian civil society organisations working with several international donors often undergo a separate due diligence assessment for each partner. Donors frequently request the same documents and review the same aspects of an organisation’s work, yet organisations cannot always use the results of an earlier assessment in a subsequent one.

Philanthropy in Ukraine examined 26 due diligence systems used by donors and international organisations in Ukraine to see how much they overlap and whether partners could recognise each other’s assessments. The findings point to opportunities for recognition under existing systems. In some cases, donors could rely on a previous assessment for most or all of their requirements.

Donors assess similar areas at different levels of detail

The team analysed the documents and requirements of all 26 systems using a common framework of 60 criteria grouped into nine thematic areas. These include organisational governance, financial capacity, safeguarding, operational processes, partner management and requirements specific to Ukraine.

The study found substantial overlap. On average, each system covered 71% of the common criteria, and five criteria appeared in all 26 systems. The level of detail varied. Some donors ask a general question about a topic, while others require specific documents, procedures and supporting evidence.

Much of the duplication stems from the way donors set out similar requirements across different documents, templates and procedures.

In 193 comparisons, one assessment covers more than 80% of another donor’s requirements

To assess where donors could recognise each other’s results in practice, the team compared each system with every other system in both directions, for a total of 650 comparisons.

  • In 193 of 650 comparisons, one donor’s assessment covers more than 80% of the other donor’s requirements.
  • In these cases, the donor accepting the earlier assessment would typically need to check about five of the roughly 40 criteria in its own system.
  • In four of these directional comparisons, the earlier assessment covers all the receiving donor’s requirements.
  • 47 donor pairs show potential for mutual recognition at a 70% coverage threshold in both directions. Six pairs meet the stricter 80% threshold.

With mutual recognition, both donors could use the results of each other’s assessments. Systems that require a similar level of detail are the strongest candidates for this approach.

The figures indicate where recognition could be possible. Each organisation would still need to decide whether to accept another donor’s assessment.

How donors could make their assessments compatible

Based on the findings, Philanthropy in Ukraine proposes a due diligence passporting approach that would allow civil society organisations to use the results of a completed assessment when working with other donors.

A standard format for assessment results would show which requirements have already been met, which need further evidence and which fell outside the scope of the earlier assessment. Digital tools could match requirements across systems and transfer documents between formats. Experts would retain responsibility for the final assessment.

Putting the approach into practice would require agreements between donors, shared rules for recognising assessments, confidence in each other’s procedures and consent from civil society organisations to use their data.

The team also developed an interactive dashboard to make the findings easier to explore. Users can compare any two due diligence systems, see where their requirements overlap or differ, examine the level of detail and identify where recognition may be possible.

item.title: MSF Myanmar: Statement ahead of the ICJ ruling on Myanmar and genocide against the Rohingya
item.description:
Countries: Myanmar, Bangladesh, Malaysia
Source: Médecins Sans Frontières

Tomorrow’s ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) will be the first time a judicial body will deliver judgment on whether Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people. This is a moment of special importance that has been long anticipated by Rohingya communities we have supported across the region for decades, including patients, colleagues, and our partners from Rohingya civil society in the diaspora. As a medical humanitarian organisation, we care for Rohingya patients in Bangladesh, Malaysia, and Myanmar — all of whom are affected by violence, displacement, and exclusion. For these patients, and for our Rohingya colleagues, recognition and justice matter. ​

In 2017, MSF published the results of a retrospective mortality survey conducted in refugee settlement camps in Bangladesh. The survey estimated that at least 9,000 Rohingya had died in Myanmar, in Rakhine state, between 25 August and 24 September. At least 71.7% of the reported deaths had been caused by violence, meaning at least 6,700 Rohingya, in the most conservative estimations, were estimated to have been killed during this brief period, including at least 730 children below the age of five years. ​

Almost 10 years later, we cannot ignore that these cycles of violence are not confined to the past. The current violence and deprivation being endured by Rohingya people is continuing to spiral. For those who remain in Rakhine State today, while the conflict dynamics are different from 2017, the crisis is ongoing: all communities are living through aerial bombardment and intense fighting between the Arakan Army and the Myanmar military, displacement, siege conditions, and the threat of forced recruitment as frontline reinforcements. For Rohingya communities specifically, long-standing discrimination and near-total restrictions on their freedom of movement compound the risks of the current conflict, leaving them particularly vulnerable to the consequences.

For those forcibly displaced across the region, they continue to face grave barriers to ensuring their safety, dignity, and access to healthcare. In Bangladesh, mass violence that erupted across the border in Myanmar in November 2023, and intensified again in April 2024, forcibly displaced 150,000 people. This brought the total number of Rohingya refugees in the Bangladesh camps to 1.2 million, placing further strain on already overburdened services. So far in 2026, more than 6,000 refugees arrived, citing forced recruitment, extortion, abduction of women and girls, land confiscation, and airstrikes as the reason for their attempt to reach safety in Bangladesh.

In Malaysia, harmful state policies leave many Rohingya at constant risk of arrest and indefinite detention, even when they are seeking medical care. At the same time, we are witnessing dangerous moves across the region toward so-called “voluntary repatriation” of refugees to Myanmar, despite conditions clearly remaining unsafe. Malaysia has already returned nearly 1,500 refugees from multiple ethnic groups, not only Rohingya. All of this is happening within a media and social media environment filled with hate speech towards Rohingya refugees, putting a target on their backs for public harassment wherever they turn. ​

Tomorrow is undoubtedly a landmark moment for Rohingya people. ​ However, it is imperative to remember that legal rulings do not resolve the immense medical and humanitarian needs that exist. There remains an urgent need for action from the Myanmar military and Arakan Army to respect international humanitarian law, immediately cease attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, and to facilitate rapid and unimpeded humanitarian assistance to those suffering the consequences. Crucially, states in the region must take action towards a zero-tolerance approach to public rhetorics of hatred, which continues to fuel violence against Rohingya refugees, driving people further away from healthcare, forcing people deeper into hiding, and in some cases, as witnessed by our team in Malaysia, pushing Rohingya people into psychiatric crisis.

The systematic persecution of Rohingya people did not end in 2017. They continue to be denied their most basic rights, including the citizenship they were stripped of in 1982. Practical, safe, and long-term solutions are urgently needed to end the physical and structural violence that, for decades, has denied Rohingya people the chance to live in safety, dignity, and freedom.
